title: Physical quantities: magnitude and unit
prior_knowledge_summary: Entry prerequisite: arithmetic, scientific notation and basic geometry from prior school mathematics.
new_learning: Every physical quantity consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit.
A numerical result must be paired with an appropriate unit when a physical quantity is reported.
not_yet_taught: SI base quantities and SI base units
Applications belonging to later Physics topics

visual_planning.reason: Six distinct visual forms make the number-unit pairing visible in a puzzle, an annotated record, a comparison, an error diagnosis and two guided calculations.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: What does 12 tell you?
content: A screen in the laboratory shows only the number 12. Does it mean a 12 s wait, a 12 m cable or a 12 kg load? The number is clear, but the measurement is not.
Now imagine the screen changes to 12 s. Predict what extra information the letter s gives you.

figure.purpose: Create the opening ambiguity that makes a unit necessary
figure.brief: Draw a laboratory display showing 12 beside three hand-drawn possibility cards: stopwatch, tape measure and mass. Then show a second display reading 12 s with only the stopwatch card remaining.
figure.alt_text: A display reading 12 could match time, length or mass, while 12 s clearly describes time.

blocks.title: A physical quantity has two parts
content: In physics, we use physical quantities to describe properties that can be measured. Every physical quantity consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit.

In the record length = 1.8 m, the numerical magnitude is 1.8 and the unit is m. The magnitude tells us how much. The unit tells us the measurement scale and helps identify what kind of quantity has been reported.
The words length, mass and time name quantities. A number and a unit report a measured value of a quantity.

figure.purpose: Show the anatomy of one reported physical quantity
figure.brief: Make an annotated measurement card reading length = 1.8 m. Use one coloured bracket under 1.8 labelled numerical magnitude and another under m labelled unit. Keep the quantity name visible but separate.
figure.alt_text: An annotated card separates length equals 1.8 m into numerical magnitude 1.8 and unit m.

blocks.title: The same number can report different quantities
content: Suppose a stopwatch record is 5 s and a ribbon length is 5 m. Both records have the same numerical magnitude, 5. They do not describe the same physical quantity because their units are different.
This is why a bare number is incomplete in a measurement record. The unit is not an optional label added after the physics. It is part of the physical quantity.

figure.purpose: Contrast equal numerical magnitudes with different units and quantities
figure.brief: Use a two-column comparison table. Left shows a stopwatch card reading 5 s. Right shows a ribbon card reading 5 m. Highlight the shared 5 in one colour and the different units in two other colours.
figure.alt_text: A stopwatch reading 5 s and a ribbon length 5 m share a magnitude but have different units.

blocks.title: A unit is not decoration
content: It can feel as if the calculation is finished when the calculator shows a number. That feels reasonable because the arithmetic has ended. But the number alone does not yet report the physical quantity.

Writing 8.4 after measuring a time leaves the reader unable to tell whether the record means seconds, metres or something else. Writing 8.4 m for that time is also wrong because an inappropriate unit changes the meaning of the record. The scientific report is complete only when the correct numerical magnitude and an appropriate unit stay together.

figure.brief: Draw three notebook entries for the same timer result: 8.4 with a question mark, 8.4 m crossed once, and 8.4 s ticked. Add sparse labels missing unit, wrong unit and complete record without revealing any later practice answer.
figure.alt_text: Notebook entries compare a missing unit, a wrong unit and a complete time record.

blocks.title: Carry the unit through a simple calculation
content: Five identical sample jars have a total mass of 3.5 kg. To find the mass of one jar, divide the total equally among the five jars.
Mass of one jar = 3.5 kg / 5 = 0.7 kg. The numerical magnitude is 0.7 and the unit is kg. The answer 0.7 alone would not report a mass.
Independent check: 5 x 0.7 kg = 3.5 kg, which agrees with the stated total mass. The arithmetic and the unit are both consistent.

figure.brief: Create an annotated three-stage layout: five identical jars on a balance reading 3.5 kg, division among five equal boxes, and one result card reading 0.7 kg with magnitude and unit bracketed separately. Include the multiplication check in a small corner box.
figure.alt_text: Five jars with total mass 3.5 kg are shared equally to give one jar a mass of 0.7 kg.

blocks.title: A second route with the same lesson
content: Six equal timing intervals have a total duration of 18 s. The duration of one interval is 18 s / 6 = 3 s.
Here the numerical magnitude is 3 and the unit is s. A separate length record could be 3 m. The shared number does not make the records interchangeable because s and m give them different meanings.
Independent check: 6 x 3 s = 18 s. The result returns to the known measurement.

figure.purpose: Reinforce number-unit pairing in a different context and representation
figure.brief: Draw a six-segment timeline labelled total 18 s, then zoom into one segment labelled 3 s. Beside it place a short ruler marked 3 m and highlight that the equal magnitudes have different units.
figure.alt_text: A timeline interval is 3 s while a ruler record is 3 m, showing equal magnitudes with different units.

blocks.title: Read every result in two passes
content: First ask: what is the numerical magnitude? Second ask: what is the unit? Keep the two together whenever you report the physical quantity.
A useful final check is to read the result aloud. If you can say only the number, the record is incomplete. If the unit describes a different kind of quantity, the record is incorrect.
Do not estimate values or classify SI units yet. This lesson builds the number-unit idea that those later lessons will use.

concepts_taught: physical quantities consist of a numerical magnitude and a unit
a bare number is incomplete as a reported physical quantity
the same numerical magnitude can occur with different units
misconceptions_addressed: a calculator number alone is a complete physical quantity
a unit is a decorative label
equal numerical magnitudes must describe the same physical quantity

report a simple calculated physical quantity with an appropriate unit
diagnose a missing or inappropriate unit
distinguish records that share a numerical magnitude but have different units
